content.text:
Answer

The following is structured content for the “Law / Elements of offence” section of an attendance note for the offence of Theft under section 1 of the Theft Act 1968 (either-way offence):

**1. Actus Reus**  
- The defendant must have *appropriated* property belonging to another.  
- “Appropriation” means assuming any of the rights of the owner, including taking or dealing with the property as if one were the owner, without consent. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/resources/common-offences/general-theft/?utm_source=openai))  
- The property must be *property* as defined by the Act (e.g., money, personal property) and must *belong to another*, meaning it is in the possession or control of someone else. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/resources/common-offences/general-theft/?utm_source=openai))  

**2. Mens Rea**  
- The appropriation must be *dishonest*. The Act does not define dishonesty fully, but section 2 provides that appropriation is not dishonest if the defendant believes they have a legal right to take it, that the owner would consent if aware, or that the owner cannot be found by taking reasonable steps. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/cy/node/5877?utm_source=openai))  
- There must be an *intention to permanently deprive* the owner of the property, meaning treating the property as one’s own to dispose of regardless of the owner’s rights. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/resources/common-offences/general-theft/?utm_source=openai))  

**3. Common Defences**  
- A genuine belief in a legal right to the property (e.g., belief that the owner would consent or cannot be found) negates dishonesty under section 2. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/cy/node/5877?utm_source=openai))  
- Lack of intention to permanently deprive (e.g., borrowing with intent to return) may negate the mens rea. (Note: this principle is well-established but not directly cited here; if needed, further case law should be sourced.)  

**4. Sentencing Guidelines Summary**  
- Theft under section 1 is triable either way, with a maximum custodial sentence of 7 years. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511&utm_source=openai))  
- The Sentencing Council’s “Theft – general” guideline (effective from 1 February 2016, updated 5 October 2026) applies. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511&utm_source=openai))  
- Sentencing involves a two-step assessment:  
  - Step 1: Determine offence category based on *harm* (financial loss and additional harm) and *culpability* (planning, role, etc.). Categories range from 1 (most serious) to 4 (least serious). ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511&utm_source=openai))  
  - Step 2: Identify the starting point and range for the category, then adjust for aggravating or mitigating factors (e.g., previous convictions, remorse, planning, vulnerability of victim). ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511&utm_source=openai))  
- Magistrates’ courts must follow these guidelines unless it would be contrary to the interests of justice. ([sentencingcouncil.org.uk](https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511&utm_source=openai))  

---

Uncertainties  
- No specific case law has been cited regarding the interpretation of “dishonesty” or “intention to permanently deprive” beyond statutory wording; further case law may be needed for nuanced analysis.  
- The guideline summary is general; specific sentencing ranges for particular categories (e.g., value thresholds) are not detailed here and would require reference to the full guideline tables.  

Sources  
1. Theft Act 1968, Section 1 – Definition of theft — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1968/60/section/1  
2. Theft – general (Sentencing Council guideline) — https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/guidelines/theft-general/?source=7511  
3. General theft (overview) — https://sentencingcouncil.org.uk/resources/common-offences/general-theft/  
4. Theft Act Offences (CPS guidance) — https://www.cps.gov.uk/cy/node/5877
